description: Southeast Asian empire (802–1431) centred on Angkor; the hydraulic civilisation of the Khmer, their vast barays (reservoirs), canal networks, and temple-mountain architecture culminating in Angkor Wat and the Bayon, supported the densest pre-industrial urban population in Southeast Asia; Devaraja cult kingship legitimised royal authority through Hindu and later Mahayana Buddhist ritual while Khmer kings extracted tribute from surrounding Cham, Mon, and Thai polities.

lifecycle_phases.description: Jayavarman II declares devaraja independence from Java; establishes Indravarman's hydraulic engineering programme around Angkor
Suryavarman II builds Angkor Wat; hydraulic civilisation supports population of 500,000–1,000,000 in the Angkor metropolitan area
Jayavarman VII conquers Champa, extends empire to Myanmar border; builds Angkor Thom with Bayon; converts to Mahayana Buddhism
Cham counterattacks; Thai Sukhothai and Ayutthaya kingdoms emerge as rivals; hydraulic system maintenance fails; repeated Ayutthayan sieges
Ayutthayan sack of Angkor ends metropolitan Khmer dominance; court retreats to Phnom Penh region

rise_factors.description: Angkor's barays (reservoirs) and canal network enabled year-round multi-crop rice agriculture supporting the highest pre-industrial urban densities in Southeast Asia
Devaraja cult, king as living god, concentrated all political and religious authority in the monarch, enabling massive corvée labour mobilisation for temple construction
Tonle Sap lake's annual flood cycle provided extraordinary fish protein and water storage that no neighbouring polity could replicate

decline_factors.description: Jayavarman VII's massive construction programme exhausted the corvée labour supply and depleted temple endowments needed to maintain hydraulic infrastructure
Thai Sukhothai and Ayutthayan kingdoms emerged from former Khmer tributary zones and proved impossible to resubordinate
